title: Estate Planning
description: A will, the forms that beat it, and a tax most families will never owe.
wolfLine: Name a guardian. Then read the beneficiary form.

will.definition: A legal document that says who should receive what you own and who should care for minor children. Beneficiary forms on accounts can override it for those accounts.
will.example: A will that names a guardian for a baby, and a retirement form that names the other parent.

power-of-attorney.definition: A document that lets someone handle your money and legal chores if you cannot. It is not a medical document.
power-of-attorney.example: The person who can pay the mortgage if you are unconscious.

health-care-directive.definition: A document that says what medical care you want if you cannot say so, and who should speak for you. It does not give that person your bank account.
health-care-directive.example: Whether you want a ventilator is a medical question, not a mortgage question.

probate.definition: The court process that settles an estate: pays debts and hands out what the will covers. It takes time, and it can be public.
probate.example: An account with a named beneficiary often skips this line and pays that person directly.

estate-tax.definition: A federal tax on very large estates. For deaths in 2026 the basic exclusion is $15,000,000. Most households never meet it. A will is still useful far below that number.
estate-tax.example: A $600,000 estate is under the 2026 exclusion.

lessons.title: Why a Will
lessons.summary: Kids and leftovers, not only fortunes.

steps.title: The document
steps.body: A [[will]] says who gets the property that does not already have a [[beneficiary]], and who cares for minor children. You do not need to be wealthy. Dying without one means the state uses a default, and that default may not be the person you would have picked. This is education, not a will you can copy from a lesson.

steps.prompt: What does a will do that a budget does not?
choices: Names who should inherit, and who should care for minor children
steps.explain: People and property. The budget is a different page.

steps.prompt: Only millionaires need a will.
steps.explain: A guardian for a child matters at any net worth. So does “not the state’s default.”

steps.prompt: Who fills in the answers if you die without a will?
steps.explain: The default. It is a real system, and it may not match your family.

steps.prompt: The legal document that names heirs and a guardian is a ___.
steps.explain: A will. The beneficiary form is a different piece of paper.

lessons.title: The Form Beats the Will
lessons.summary: For that account, the name on the form is the heir.

steps.title: Two pieces of paper
steps.body: Retirement accounts and life insurance pay the [[beneficiary]] named on the form. If the form says Alex and the [[will]] says Sam, Alex gets this account. The will still matters for the house, the stuff, and a guardian. It does not silently correct an old form.

steps.prompt: On this account, the will overrides the beneficiary form.
steps.explain: The form pays Alex. The will’s Sam does not replace that name. Update the form itself.

doc.title: Retirement account form
doc.subtitle: The form wins for this account
doc.note: For this account, the named beneficiary is paid. The will does not override that name.

steps.prompt: How many dollars are on the account the form controls?
steps.explain: The balance is $80,000, and it follows the beneficiary, not the conflicting sentence in the will.

steps.prompt: You remarry and forget the old form. What happens to this account?
choices: It pays whoever the form still names
It automatically switches to the new spouse
steps.explain: The form stays until you change it. A wedding does not edit it.

steps.prompt: What should you do after a marriage, a divorce, or a birth?
choices: Read every beneficiary form and update the stale ones
Assume the will covers the accounts
Close the accounts so the question disappears
steps.explain: Read the forms. The will cannot reach through them.

lessons.title: Money, and Medicine
lessons.summary: Two documents. Do not swap them.

steps.title: Different jobs
steps.body: A [[power of attorney]] lets someone handle money if you cannot. A [[health care directive]] says what care you want and who speaks to the doctors. One person can be both, but the papers are not substitutes. A medical document does not pay the mortgage. A financial document does not choose a ventilator.

steps.prompt: Which document is this job?
items: Paying the mortgage if you are unconscious
Saying whether you want a ventilator
Talking to the bank about your bills
Talking to the doctors about your care
steps.explain: Money and bills are the power of attorney. Care choices are the health care directive.

steps.prompt: A health care directive lets that person empty your brokerage.
steps.explain: Medical wishes only. The money document is the power of attorney.

steps.prompt: Why have both, even if one trusted person would do either job?
choices: Because banks and hospitals look for different papers
Because the Fed requires a pair
steps.explain: Each institution wants the paper that matches its job.

steps.prompt: The document for medical wishes is a health care ___.
steps.explain: Directive. The power of attorney is the money one.

steps.title: The container
steps.body: A trust is a legal container that can hold assets. Property in the trust can skip [[probate]]. A trust does not replace a [[will]] for the things left outside it, and it does not name a guardian unless the papers say so. People use trusts for control and for privacy. This lesson will not build one or promise a tax result.

steps.prompt: What is a trust, at this level?
choices: A required replacement for a will
steps.explain: A container. The will still has work, especially for anything the trust does not hold.

steps.prompt: Putting nothing into the trust still keeps those assets out of probate.
steps.explain: Only what the trust actually holds can skip probate that way. An empty trust holds nothing.

steps.prompt: What is a fair reason people look at a trust?
choices: To control how assets pass, and sometimes to skip probate
steps.explain: Control and probate. It is not a higher withdrawal rate, and the beneficiary forms still matter.

steps.prompt: A legal container that can hold assets is a ___.
steps.explain: A trust. It holds only what you actually put in it.

lessons.title: Probate
lessons.summary: The court, the debts, the leftovers.

steps.title: The process
steps.body: [[Probate]] is the court process that pays the estate’s debts and hands out what the [[will]] covers. It takes months, it costs money, and it can be public. Accounts with a beneficiary, and assets actually held in a trust, often skip that line. The house in your own name often does not.

steps.prompt: What is probate?
choices: The court process that settles the estate
steps.explain: Court, debts, and distribution. Not a fund and not a bracket.

steps.prompt: Every asset you own must go through probate, including life insurance with a living beneficiary.
steps.explain: A living beneficiary on the policy is paid directly. Probate is for what does not already have a path.

steps.prompt: Which asset is the classic probate candidate?
choices: A house titled only in your name, with no transfer set up
A retirement account with a living beneficiary
Life insurance payable to a named person
steps.explain: The house in your name alone. The named-beneficiary accounts have their own path.

steps.prompt: A probate example costs $3,000 in court and legal fees on a $60,000 estate that had to go through it. What percent of that estate is the $3,000?
steps.explain: $3,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.05, which is 5%. Small estates feel the fee. This is an example cost, not a quote.

lessons.title: Where Everything Is
lessons.summary: A list the living person can actually find.

steps.title: The unglamorous page
steps.body: The best papers fail if nobody can find them. Write where the accounts are, who the [[beneficiary]] is, where the [[will]] is, and tell the person who would have to use the list. A password in your head is not a plan.

steps.prompt: Put the “where everything is” list in order.
items: List each account and the institution that holds it
Write the beneficiary named on each account
Note where the will and the directives are kept
Tell the person who would have to open the list
steps.explain: The accounts, then the names on them, then the location of the papers, then a living person who knows.

steps.prompt: A list that only you can find is enough.
steps.explain: Someone else has to use it. If it is a secret, it is not a plan.

steps.prompt: What belongs next to each account on the list?
choices: Your hope about who should inherit
steps.explain: The name on the form, not the name you meant to write later.

steps.prompt: The list fails if the person who needs it cannot ___ it.
steps.explain: Find it. Tell them, and keep the page somewhere they can open.

lessons.title: The Estate Tax
lessons.summary: A 2026 exclusion most families never touch.

steps.title: The large-number tax
steps.body: The federal [[estate tax]] applies to very large estates. For deaths in 2026 the basic exclusion is $15,000,000. A $600,000 estate is under it, so this lesson’s ordinary household does not owe federal estate tax. A state can have its own tax. This course will not grade a state amount. The will, the guardian, and the beneficiary forms matter long before $15,000,000.

steps.prompt: What is the 2026 federal basic exclusion, in dollars?
steps.explain: The 2026 basic exclusion is $15,000,000. It is a federal figure for that year.

steps.prompt: A $600,000 estate owes federal estate tax in 2026 under this exclusion.
steps.explain: $600,000 is far under $15,000,000. The federal estate tax is not why this household needs a will.

steps.prompt: Why does a family under the exclusion still need a will?
choices: Guardians, and property the beneficiary forms do not cover
To create a federal estate-tax bill
steps.explain: Children and the leftovers. The tax is a different problem, for a different size of estate.

steps.prompt: What will this course not do?
choices: Grade a state’s estate or inheritance tax
Tell you a beneficiary form can beat a will
steps.explain: State rules differ. The federal exclusion is the number this lesson will stand behind.

lessons.title: The Lees, After the Baby
lessons.summary: A new person, so the papers change.

story.title: After the baby
story.body:
The Lees’ net worth is about **$400,000**. The 2026 federal estate-tax exclusion is **$15,000,000**, so the tax is not their project.

The baby is. The will needs a guardian, and the beneficiary forms need a look.

steps.title: Meet the Lees
steps.body:
The Lees just had a baby. Their net worth is about $400,000, mostly home equity and savings. That is under the 2026 federal estate-tax exclusion of $15,000,000, so the tax is not their project.

The project is the baby. The [[will]] needs a guardian. The retirement [[beneficiary]] forms need a look. The life insurance form needs the same look. They tell one trusted person where the papers are.

steps.prompt: The Lees can skip a will because $400,000 is under the 2026 exclusion.
steps.explain: The exclusion answers the federal estate tax. It does not name a guardian for the baby.

steps.prompt: How far under $15,000,000 is a $400,000 estate, in dollars?
steps.explain: $15,000,000 − $400,000 = $14,600,000 under the exclusion. The gap is the point: the tax is not their problem.

steps.prompt: What is the first paper the baby changes?
choices: The will, so a guardian is named
steps.explain: A guardian. The funds can wait. The baby cannot.

steps.prompt: Put the Lees’ afternoon in order.
items: Name a guardian in the will
Read the beneficiary forms on retirement and life insurance
Update any form that is stale
Tell one trusted person where the papers are
steps.explain: The guardian, then the forms, then a living person who can find the stack.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Estate Planning
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A life insurance beneficiary form loses to a conflicting sentence in the will.
steps.explain: The form pays the named beneficiary. Change the form if the name is wrong.

steps.prompt: What is the 2026 federal estate-tax basic exclusion, in dollars?
steps.explain: The 2026 basic exclusion is $15,000,000.

steps.prompt: Paying bills if you are unconscious belongs on which document?
steps.explain: Money is the power of attorney. Medical wishes are the health care directive.

steps.prompt: An empty trust keeps your house out of probate.
steps.explain: The trust only helps assets it actually holds. A house still in your name is a probate candidate.
